Modifier Same class Same package Subclass other package Everywhere
private Yes No No No
package-private Yes Yes No No
protected Yes Yes Yes No
public Yes Yes Yes Yes
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Making fields public, using protected as "less public", exposing implementation classes from shared modules, and widening visibility just to make tests easier are common design leaks.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. How does package-private differ from protected?
  2. Can the JVM reject access even if bytecode exists?
  3. Why should shared library APIs minimize public surface area?
  4. How do access modifiers support encapsulation in Spring services?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • private protects invariants.
  • package-private is excellent for internal package design.
  • protected is for inheritance contracts, not general sharing.
  • public is a long-term API commitment.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Encapsulation and API boundaries
JVM Access flags and verifier checks
Performance No meaningful steady-state cost
Architecture Keep contracts small and intentional

Practice — Lesson 11

Refactor a service package so only facade classes are public, helper classes are package-private, fields are private final, and tests verify behavior through public contracts instead of internal state.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Packages group related Java types under a namespace. They organize code, prevent class-name collisions, define package-private visibility boundaries, and map source structure to runtime class identity.

com.acme.orders
  |-- api
  |-- domain
  |-- persistence
Part 2

History

Packages have existed since early Java to support internet-scale naming. The reverse-DNS convention, such as com.company.product, reduced collisions across libraries downloaded from many vendors.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Enterprise applications contain thousands of classes. Without packages, names collide, code ownership is unclear, and the compiler cannot distinguish domain boundaries.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java packages provide namespaces, access-control boundaries, class loading identity, documentation structure, and a clean way to publish APIs.

Part 5

Internal Working

The package declaration becomes part of the binary class name. com.acme.OrderService is distinct from com.other.OrderService even if both simple class names match.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

The JVM identifies classes by fully qualified binary name plus defining class loader. Packages are not directories to the JVM; they are name prefixes embedded in class metadata.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Packages do not change object memory layout. They affect metadata, class lookup paths, and access checks.

ClassLoader
  -> com/acme/orders/OrderService.class
  -> java/lang/String.class
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Compiler reads package.
  2. Imports resolve simple names.
  3. Bytecode references fully qualified names.
  4. Class loader locates matching class resource.
  5. JVM links and initializes the class.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Package organization has minimal direct runtime cost. Poor package design increases build time, classpath size, and cognitive load.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Name resolution during compilation depends on imports and classpath/module path size. Runtime class lookup is implementation-dependent but typically optimized by class loader caches.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Fully qualified names add metadata bytes in class files and constant pools. Runtime object size is unaffected.

Part 12

Code Examples

package com.acme.orders.domain;

public final class Order {
    private final OrderId id;

    public Order(OrderId id) {
        this.id = id;
    }

    public OrderId id() {
        return id;
    }
}

package com.acme.orders.api;

import com.acme.orders.domain.Order;

public record OrderResponse(String id) {
    public static OrderResponse from(Order order) {
        return new OrderResponse(order.id().value());
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Common production layouts use packages by layer (controller, service, repository) or by feature (orders.api, orders.domain, orders.persistence). Feature packages scale better when services grow into multiple bounded contexts.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring Boot component scanning starts from the application class package by default. Put the main class at a root package above controllers, services, repositories, and configuration.

package com.acme.orders;

@SpringBootApplication
public class OrdersApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrdersApplication.class, args);
    }
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Microservices should use packages that mirror bounded contexts and deployment ownership. Avoid sharing package names across services unless publishing a deliberate shared library.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Package design is architectural communication. A good package tree shows ownership, dependency direction, and public contracts before anyone reads method bodies.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Situation Package strategy Reason
Small CRUD app Layered Simple and familiar
Domain-heavy service Feature/bounded context Reduces cross-feature coupling
Shared SDK API/internal split Protects compatibility
JPMS module Export only API packages Strong runtime encapsulation
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Approach Strength Risk
Layer packages Easy onboarding Feature logic scattered
Feature packages Strong cohesion Needs discipline
Technical packages only Familiar Encourages anemic domain model
API/internal packages Clear contracts Requires thoughtful boundaries
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Using the default package, putting the Spring Boot main class too deep, creating vague packages like common and utils, and allowing circular package dependencies are common long-term maintenance problems.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. Why is a package part of class identity?
  2. How does package-private access influence design?
  3. Why does Spring Boot package placement matter?
  4. How would you organize a domain-heavy microservice?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Packages are namespaces and visibility boundaries.
  • Fully qualified class names appear in bytecode.
  • Class identity also includes the class loader.
  • Package structure should reveal architecture.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Namespace Avoids class-name collision
Visibility Enables package-private design
Spring Controls default component scanning
Architecture Reflects bounded contexts

Practice — Lesson 12

Design package names for an orders service with API, domain, persistence, messaging, and configuration concerns. Identify which packages should expose public classes and which should remain internal.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Enums model a fixed set of named constants with type safety. Unlike integer constants, Java enums are real classes with fields, methods, constructors, interfaces, and controlled instances.

PaymentStatus
  +-- AUTHORIZED
  +-- CAPTURED
  +-- FAILED
Part 2

History

Java introduced enums in Java 5. Before that, developers used integer or string constants, which were error-prone and lacked compiler-enforced type safety.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Status values, modes, and categories often have finite valid values. Strings allow typos, integers hide meaning, and both make refactoring dangerous.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Enums give readable constants, exhaustive switch support, serialization identity, singleton-like instance control, and the ability to attach behavior to fixed values.

Part 5

Internal Working

Each enum constant is a singleton instance of the enum class. The compiler generates values(), valueOf(String), ordinal handling, and static initialization code.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

An enum compiles to a final class extending java.lang.Enum. Constants are static final fields. Developers cannot directly extend Enum.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Enum instances live as static objects referenced by the enum class. Each instance stores fields declared by the enum plus inherited name and ordinal.

PaymentStatus.class
  static AUTHORIZED -> enum object
  static CAPTURED   -> enum object
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Enum class initializes.
  2. Constants are constructed once.
  3. values() returns an array of constants.
  4. switch compiles to efficient dispatch using generated mapping or ordinal logic.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Enum comparison with == is fast and safe. EnumSet and EnumMap are highly optimized because they use ordinal-based bit vectors or arrays internally.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Enum comparison is O(1). EnumMap access is O(1). values() is O(n) because it returns a cloned array.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Enum space is O(n) for n constants. EnumSet is compact, often using one long for up to 64 constants.

Part 12

Code Examples

public enum PaymentStatus {
    AUTHORIZED(true),
    CAPTURED(true),
    FAILED(false);

    private final boolean billable;

    PaymentStatus(boolean billable) {
        this.billable = billable;
    }

    public boolean isBillable() {
        return billable;
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Enums are used for order status, retry strategy, feature flag state, identity-provider type, and workflow stage. Persist stable names, not ordinals, because ordinal changes corrupt meaning.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring MVC can bind request parameters to enums, and Jackson can serialize enum names. Use explicit JSON values when public APIs need stable external names.

@GetMapping("/payments")
public List<PaymentDto> findByStatus(@RequestParam PaymentStatus status) {
    return service.findByStatus(status);
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Enums in service internals are safe. Enums in public API contracts require versioning discipline because adding or renaming values can break clients.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Use enums for genuinely closed sets. If product teams can add values dynamically, use database-backed reference data instead of redeploying code for each new value.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Use enum? Reason
Fixed workflow status Yes Compiler-enforced values
User-created category No Runtime extensibility needed
Bitwise permissions Maybe EnumSet works well
External partner codes Carefully Need stable mapping
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Option Type safe Extensible at runtime Behavior support
String constants No Yes No
Integer constants No Yes No
Enum Yes No Yes
Database reference table Some Yes Externalized
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Persisting ordinals, exposing enum names without API governance, using enums for open business catalogs, and putting too much unrelated business logic in enum constants are frequent mistakes.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. Why should enum ordinals not be persisted?
  2. How does EnumSet achieve compact storage?
  3. Can enums have constructors and fields?
  4. When should an enum be replaced by reference data?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Java enums are classes with fixed instances.
  • Compare enums with ==.
  • Persist stable names or explicit codes, not ordinals.
  • Use EnumSet and EnumMap for enum-keyed collections.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Type safety Prevents invalid constant values
JVM Static singleton enum objects
Collections EnumSet and EnumMap are optimized
Architecture Best for closed sets

Practice — Lesson 13

Create an enum-backed payment state machine. Add a method that lists allowed transitions, then decide whether each state belongs in code, a database table, or an external contract.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Wrapper classes represent primitive values as objects: Integer, Long, Boolean, Double, and others. Autoboxing converts primitives to wrappers, while unboxing converts wrappers back to primitives.

int 42  --boxing-->  Integer(42)
Integer(42) --unboxing--> int 42
Part 2

History

Java 1.0 separated primitives from objects for performance. Java 5 introduced autoboxing so generics and collections could work more ergonomically with primitive values.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Collections and generic APIs work with object references, not primitives. Before autoboxing, developers wrote verbose conversions like Integer.valueOf(count).

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Wrappers bridge primitive performance with object-oriented APIs. They also provide constants, parsing helpers, comparison methods, and nullable representations.

Part 5

Internal Working

The compiler inserts calls such as Integer.valueOf(x) for boxing and integer.intValue() for unboxing. Autoboxing is syntactic convenience, not a new runtime type.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

The JVM executes normal method calls and reference operations. Wrapper caches, such as Integer values from -128 to 127, are implemented by library classes, not special bytecode.

Part 7

Memory Layout

A primitive local may live directly in a stack slot or register. A wrapper is an object with a header and value field, referenced from variables or collections.

List<Integer>
  [ref] -> Integer object header + int value
  [ref] -> Integer object header + int value
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Primitive is assigned to wrapper variable.
  2. Compiler emits valueOf.
  3. Cached object may be reused.
  4. Wrapper used in collection or API call.
  5. Unboxing emits primitive accessor call.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Boxing can allocate objects, increase GC pressure, and add null checks. JIT escape analysis may eliminate some allocations, but hot paths should prefer primitives or primitive-specialized libraries.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Boxing and unboxing are O(1). Collection operations remain their normal complexity, but boxing increases constants and memory traffic.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Primitive arrays are compact. Wrapper collections require one reference per element plus one object per uncached value, producing much larger memory footprints.

Part 12

Code Examples

List<Integer> ids = new ArrayList<>();
ids.add(42);          // autoboxes to Integer.valueOf(42)
int first = ids.get(0); // unboxes with intValue()

Integer missing = null;
// int value = missing; // NullPointerException during unboxing
Part 13

Real Production Examples

DTOs often use wrappers for optional JSON fields: Integer retryCount can distinguish missing from zero. Internal counters should usually use primitives unless null has domain meaning.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Configuration properties and request bodies often use wrappers to represent optional values. Validation annotations can then express requirements explicitly.

public record RetryProperties(
        @Min(0) Integer maxAttempts,
        Boolean enabled
) {}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

In microservice APIs, wrapper nullability must be documented. Integer quantity can mean absent, unknown, or zero depending on contract; ambiguity causes downstream bugs.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Use primitives for required internal values and wrappers for boundary nullability. Avoid letting transport-layer null semantics leak into core domain models.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Choose Reason
Required count int Compact and non-null
Optional API field Integer Can represent absence
Large numeric array primitive array Avoid wrapper overhead
Generic collection wrapper Required by Java generics
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Aspect Primitive Wrapper
Nullable No Yes
Object identity No Yes, but rarely useful
Collection support Not directly Yes
Memory footprint Low Higher
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Comparing wrappers with ==, unboxing null values, using wrappers in hot loops unnecessarily, and assuming all boxed integers are cached are common production defects.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. What bytecode pattern does autoboxing create?
  2. Why can unboxing throw NullPointerException?
  3. Why is Integer a = 128; a == b unreliable?
  4. When should wrappers be used in API DTOs?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Autoboxing is compiler-inserted conversion.
  • Wrapper identity is not value equality.
  • Use equals or primitive comparison after null checks.
  • Wrappers are useful for nullable boundaries.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Bridge primitives and object APIs
JVM Normal objects and method calls
Performance Boxing may allocate and increase GC
Architecture Be explicit about null semantics

Practice — Lesson 14

Inspect a DTO, entity, and domain class. Decide which numeric and boolean fields should be primitive or wrapper, then document what null means for each wrapper field.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Generics let classes, interfaces, and methods operate on parameterized types. They improve type safety and remove many casts while preserving a single reusable implementation.

Repository<T>
  +-- Repository<Order>
  +-- Repository<Customer>
Part 2

History

Generics arrived in Java 5. They were implemented with type erasure to remain binary-compatible with existing Java libraries and the JVM.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Before generics, collections stored Object, forcing casts at call sites. Type mistakes appeared at runtime as ClassCastException rather than at compile time.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Generics provide compile-time type safety, reusable abstractions, expressive API contracts, and cleaner code for collections, repositories, handlers, and factories.

Part 5

Internal Working

The compiler checks generic types, inserts casts where needed, and erases most type parameters in bytecode. List<String> and List<Integer> are both mostly List at runtime.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Generic signatures are stored as metadata, but execution uses erased types. Bounded type parameters erase to their first bound; unbounded parameters erase to Object.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Generics do not create specialized object layouts. A List<String> and List<Order> use the same collection implementation storing object references.

ArrayList elementData
  [ref] [ref] [ref]
       runtime objects keep their own classes
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Compiler validates type parameters.
  2. Type arguments are erased.
  3. Bridge methods may be generated for polymorphism.
  4. Runtime executes erased bytecode.
  5. Casts protect values read from generic structures.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Generics themselves do not add polymorphic specialization overhead. However, primitive values still require boxing in generic collections, which can affect hot paths.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Generics do not change algorithmic complexity. List<T>.get(index) remains O(1) for ArrayList and O(n) for LinkedList.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Generic metadata adds class-file signature information. Runtime collections store references, not type-specific inline values.

Part 12

Code Examples

public interface Repository<T, ID> {
    Optional<T> findById(ID id);
    T save(T entity);
}

public final class OrderRepository implements Repository<Order, OrderId> {
    public Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id) {
        return Optional.empty();
    }

    public Order save(Order entity) {
        return entity;
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Generics appear in Spring Data repositories, event handlers, mappers, API responses, cache wrappers, and retry templates. They reduce duplication across domain types while preserving compile-time guarantees.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring uses generics in JpaRepository<T, ID>, ResponseEntity<T>, ApplicationListener<E>, and dependency injection. Generic type metadata can influence bean resolution.

public interface OrderJpaRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderEntity, UUID> {
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Generic response envelopes can standardize pagination and error metadata, but over-generic APIs can hide domain intent. Keep external contracts readable.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Generics are best for infrastructure abstractions with stable behavior across types. Avoid generic designs that require many unsafe casts or make the domain language harder to understand.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Generic design? Reason
Repository interface Yes Same behavior by entity type
Domain policy with unique rules Maybe Avoid hiding business language
Utility mapper Yes Reusable type-safe conversion
Public REST schema Carefully Explicit contracts matter
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Feature Benefit Limitation
Type parameter Reuse and safety Erased at runtime
Wildcard ? extends Read covariance Cannot safely add
Wildcard ? super Write contravariance Reads are less specific
Bounds Express constraints Can become complex
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Using raw types, misunderstanding List<Object> versus List<String>, overusing wildcards in public APIs, and expecting new T() or T.class to work after erasure are common mistakes.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. What is type erasure?
  2. Why is List<String> not a subtype of List<Object>?
  3. Explain PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
  4. Why can generic arrays be problematic?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Generics are mostly compile-time safety.
  • Runtime uses erased bytecode.
  • Use ? extends T for producers and ? super T for consumers.
  • Avoid raw types except when integrating legacy APIs.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Type-safe reusable abstractions
JVM Implemented through erasure
Performance No specialization; boxing still matters
Architecture Use where abstraction clarifies intent

Practice — Lesson 15

Create a generic CommandHandler<C, R> interface and two concrete handlers. Add a method that accepts List<? extends Command> and explain why adding new commands to that list is unsafe.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Annotations attach metadata to code elements such as classes, methods, fields, parameters, and type uses. They do not directly execute behavior; tools, compilers, frameworks, or runtime reflection interpret them.

@RestController
class OrderController { ... }
        |
        +-- metadata read by Spring
Part 2

History

Annotations were introduced in Java 5 to replace external XML descriptors and marker interfaces for many metadata-driven use cases.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Frameworks need a way to associate configuration with code without scattering separate files. Developers need metadata that stays close to the element it describes.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides annotations for compile-time checks, code generation, documentation, dependency injection, validation, serialization, persistence mapping, and runtime framework discovery.

Part 5

Internal Working

Annotations are defined with @interface. Their retention policy controls where they survive: source only, class file, or runtime reflection.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Class files store annotation attributes such as RuntimeVisibleAnnotations and RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations. Runtime-retained annotations can be read through reflection APIs.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Annotations do not change object instance layout. They add metadata to class files and may create runtime proxy objects when accessed reflectively.

Class metadata
  +-- fields
  +-- methods
  +-- runtime annotations
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Compiler parses annotation usage.
  2. Annotation processors may run.
  3. Class file stores retained metadata.
  4. Framework scans classes.
  5. Framework applies behavior based on metadata.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Annotation presence is cheap. Classpath scanning and reflective annotation reading can be expensive at startup, especially in large Spring applications.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Reading a known annotation from a known element is near O(1) after metadata lookup. Scanning all classes is O(n) in the number of classes and members inspected.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Annotations add class-file metadata. Runtime frameworks may build indexes or bean definitions, increasing startup memory.

Part 12

Code Examples

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface Audited {
    String action();
}

public class PaymentService {
    @Audited(action = "capture-payment")
    public void capture(String paymentId) {
        // business logic
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Annotations drive JPA mappings, Bean Validation, Jackson JSON binding, OpenAPI documentation, Micrometer metrics, test configuration, and security rules.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring Boot relies heavily on annotations such as @SpringBootApplication, @Bean, @Component, @Transactional, @ConfigurationProperties, and @PreAuthorize.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderResponse get(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        return new OrderResponse(id.toString());
    }
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Annotations can standardize cross-cutting concerns: tracing, validation, rate limiting, idempotency, and authorization. Keep annotation semantics explicit so teams do not rely on hidden magic.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Annotations make simple cases elegant but can obscure control flow. Architects should document custom annotations, test their processors/aspects, and avoid business behavior that is invisible to code readers.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Annotation fit Reason
Declarative validation Strong Metadata maps well
Complex workflow logic Weak Hidden execution path
Compile-time generated mapper Strong Processor can verify
Runtime dynamic rule Maybe External config may be clearer
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Retention Available in source In class file At runtime
SOURCE Yes No No
CLASS Yes Yes No
RUNTIME Yes Yes Yes
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Using runtime retention unnecessarily, creating unclear custom annotations, forgetting annotation targets, assuming annotations execute by themselves, and overusing annotations where plain code would be clearer are common problems.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. What is the difference between SOURCE, CLASS, and RUNTIME retention?
  2. How do annotation processors differ from reflection?
  3. Why can Spring annotation scanning affect startup time?
  4. Can annotations contain arbitrary object fields?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Annotations are metadata.
  • Retention controls lifecycle.
  • Frameworks interpret annotations.
  • Annotation processors run during compilation.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Declarative metadata
JVM Stored as class-file attributes
Performance Startup scanning can matter
Architecture Use for clear cross-cutting contracts

Practice — Lesson 16

Create a custom @Idempotent annotation for command handlers. Define its retention, target, and expected framework behavior, then explain whether it should be implemented by AOP, filter logic, or explicit service code.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Reflection lets Java code inspect and sometimes modify classes, constructors, methods, fields, annotations, and generic metadata at runtime.

Class<?> type
  +-- constructors
  +-- methods
  +-- fields
  +-- annotations
Part 2

History

Reflection has existed since early Java to support dynamic tools, IDEs, debuggers, serializers, and frameworks. It became central to enterprise Java and Spring-style dependency injection.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Frameworks often need to operate on user-defined classes without compile-time knowledge. A JSON mapper, ORM, or DI container must discover structure dynamically.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides reflection for dynamic inspection, framework integration, tooling, serialization, testing, and runtime adapters.

Part 5

Internal Working

Reflection APIs read JVM class metadata. Invocation through reflection performs access checks unless overridden, argument adaptation, and method dispatch through reflective infrastructure.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

The JVM exposes metadata through java.lang.Class and java.lang.reflect. Modern JDKs use method handles and generated accessors internally for some reflective operations.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Reflection does not alter instance layout, but reflective metadata objects and caches consume heap memory. Frameworks often cache resolved members aggressively.

Application heap
  +-- service objects
  +-- reflection metadata cache
  +-- generated proxies
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Obtain Class<?>.
  2. Locate constructor, method, or field.
  3. Validate accessibility.
  4. Invoke or read/write reflectively.
  5. Convert or propagate checked exceptions.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Reflective invocation is slower than direct calls, especially before warmup. The biggest production cost is often startup scanning and metadata construction, not individual reflective calls.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Looking up members by name is typically O(n) over declared members unless cached. Invoking a resolved method is O(1) with a higher constant than direct invocation.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with discovered metadata, generated proxies, and caches. Large applications can spend meaningful memory on framework reflection caches.

Part 12

Code Examples

Class<?> type = Class.forName("com.acme.orders.OrderCreatedEvent");
Object event = type.getConstructor(String.class).newInstance("order-123");

Method method = type.getMethod("orderId");
Object orderId = method.invoke(event);
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Reflection powers Jackson property discovery, Hibernate entity mapping, Spring dependency injection, test frameworks, OpenAPI generation, and migration tools.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring uses reflection to instantiate beans, invoke lifecycle callbacks, read annotations, create proxies, and bind configuration. Spring AOT reduces reflection for native images.

@Component
public class StartupProbe {
    @PostConstruct
    void validate() {
        // Spring discovers and invokes this lifecycle method.
    }
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Reflection is acceptable in infrastructure paths, but avoid reflection-heavy logic in latency-critical request loops. Native-image deployments require explicit reflection configuration or AOT support.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Reflection trades compile-time clarity for runtime flexibility. Use it behind framework or library boundaries, cache resolved metadata, and prefer explicit code for domain rules.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Reflection? Reason
JSON binding Yes Dynamic DTO discovery
Domain validation rule Usually no Explicit code is clearer
Plugin loading Yes Runtime discovery
Hot request computation Avoid Higher overhead and fragility
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Approach Strength Weakness
Direct call Fast, type-safe Static binding
Reflection Flexible Slower, less safe
Method handles Faster dynamic access More complex
Code generation Fast at runtime Build complexity
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Repeated member lookup in hot paths, breaking encapsulation with setAccessible(true), ignoring JPMS restrictions, swallowing reflective exceptions, and forgetting native-image reflection config are common issues.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. Why is reflection slower than direct invocation?
  2. What does setAccessible(true) do and why is it risky?
  3. How do JPMS modules affect reflection?
  4. Why does GraalVM native image care about reflection?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Reflection inspects runtime metadata.
  • Cache reflective lookups.
  • Keep reflection out of core domain logic.
  • JPMS and native images constrain reflective access.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Runtime inspection and invocation
JVM Uses class metadata and reflective APIs
Performance Startup and lookup costs matter
Architecture Hide behind infrastructure boundaries

Practice — Lesson 17

Write a small reflective mapper from a record to a Map<String, Object>. Then identify what should be cached, what exceptions need handling, and whether the mapper would work in a native-image deployment.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Records are compact classes for transparent, shallowly immutable data carriers. A record declares its state in the header and receives generated accessors, constructor, equals, hashCode, and toString.

record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency)
       |      |
       |      +-- component
       +-- data carrier contract
Part 2

History

Records became a standard feature in Java 16 after preview releases. They addressed boilerplate-heavy DTO and value-object patterns.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Plain data classes often repeat constructors, getters, equality, and string representation. Manual implementations create bugs and distract from domain meaning.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides records to express data-as-data, reduce boilerplate, improve readability, and support pattern matching and modern immutable API design.

Part 5

Internal Working

A record extends java.lang.Record. Components define private final fields, public accessor methods, and a canonical constructor. You can add validation in a compact constructor.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Record metadata is stored in the class file. Reflection can identify records and their components through Class::isRecord and getRecordComponents.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Records are ordinary objects with fields. They are not value types and do not automatically avoid object headers or references.

Record object
  header
  final amount reference
  final currency reference
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Constructor receives component values.
  2. Compact constructor validation runs if declared.
  3. Fields are assigned.
  4. Accessors return component values.
  5. Generated equality compares component values.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Records have performance similar to equivalent final classes. Their main benefit is correctness and clarity, not lower allocation cost.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Accessor calls are O(1). Generated equals and hashCode are O(n) in component count and component comparison cost.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space is equivalent to a class with the same fields. Shallow immutability means referenced mutable objects can still change.

Part 12

Code Examples

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
    public Money {
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        if (amount.signum() < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be non-negative");
        }
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Records are useful for API responses, command objects, domain value objects, projection results, event payloads, and test fixtures.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring Boot supports records for request bodies, responses, configuration properties, and projections when constructors and JSON binding are compatible.

public record CreateOrderRequest(UUID customerId, List<LineItemRequest> items) {
}

@PostMapping("/orders")
public OrderResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
    return service.create(request);
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Records work well for immutable message payloads and DTOs. Avoid exposing records directly if external contracts need backward-compatible evolution with optional fields and custom serialization names.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Records are excellent for value semantics. They are poor fits for mutable JPA entities, lifecycle-heavy aggregates, or classes requiring identity separate from state.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Use record? Reason
Immutable DTO Yes Low boilerplate
JPA entity Usually no Framework requires mutable lifecycle
Domain value object Yes Equality by state
Stateful service No Behavior and dependencies dominate
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Type Boilerplate Mutability Equality
POJO High Flexible Manual
Lombok data class Low Configurable Generated
Record Very low Shallow immutable Generated by components
JPA entity Medium Mutable Identity-focused
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Using records for entities, assuming deep immutability, placing too much behavior in DTO records, exposing mutable collections without defensive copies, and expecting JavaBean getter names are common issues.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. What methods does a record generate?
  2. Are records deeply immutable?
  3. Why are records usually bad JPA entities?
  4. How can compact constructors validate data?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Records model transparent data carriers.
  • Components define fields and accessors.
  • Records are ordinary objects, not value types.
  • Use defensive copies for mutable components.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Concise immutable data carriers
JVM Extends java.lang.Record
Performance Similar to equivalent class
Architecture Great for DTOs and value objects

Practice — Lesson 18

Convert a request DTO and a domain value object to records. Add compact constructor validation and decide whether any collection components need defensive copying.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Sealed classes and interfaces restrict which types may extend or implement them. They model closed hierarchies while still allowing polymorphism.

sealed interface PaymentResult
  permits Approved, Declined, PendingReview
Part 2

History

Sealed classes became standard in Java 17 after preview releases. They support domain modeling and pattern matching by making permitted subtypes explicit.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Traditional inheritance is open by default. When a domain hierarchy should have only known variants, open extension makes exhaustive handling impossible and weakens invariants.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides sealed types to encode closed sets of behavior-rich variants, support safer switch/pattern matching, and improve API control.

Part 5

Internal Working

A sealed type declares permitted subclasses. Each permitted subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed, explicitly choosing whether extension stops or continues.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Class files store permitted subclass metadata. The JVM verifies that only permitted classes extend sealed parents.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Sealing does not change object layout. Each subtype has its own normal class layout and vtable behavior.

PaymentResult ref
  -> Approved object
  -> Declined object
  -> PendingReview object
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Compiler validates permitted subtype declarations.
  2. Subclasses declare final, sealed, or non-sealed.
  3. Bytecode stores permitted subclass information.
  4. JVM verifies inheritance during class loading.
  5. Pattern matching can reason about exhaustive variants.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

Sealed types primarily improve correctness and modeling. The JIT may benefit from narrower type hierarchies, but design clarity is the main value.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Sealing does not change algorithmic complexity. Dispatch and pattern matching remain dependent on generated bytecode and subtype count.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Permitted-subclass metadata adds small class-file overhead. Runtime object size is unchanged.

Part 12

Code Examples

public sealed interface PaymentResult
        permits PaymentResult.Approved, PaymentResult.Declined, PaymentResult.PendingReview {

    record Approved(String authorizationId) implements PaymentResult {}

    record Declined(String reasonCode) implements PaymentResult {}

    record PendingReview(String caseId) implements PaymentResult {}
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Sealed hierarchies work well for command outcomes, domain errors, workflow states, authorization decisions, and integration responses with known variants.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring applications can use sealed interfaces for service results and map them to HTTP responses centrally. Jackson polymorphic serialization needs explicit configuration.

PaymentResult result = paymentService.capture(command);

return switch (result) {
    case PaymentResult.Approved approved -> ResponseEntity.ok(approved);
    case PaymentResult.Declined declined -> ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(declined);
    case PaymentResult.PendingReview review -> ResponseEntity.accepted().body(review);
};
Part 15

Microservice Usage

For internal service logic, sealed results reduce exception-driven flow. For public contracts, be cautious because adding a permitted subtype can require all consumers to handle a new variant.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Sealed classes are a strong domain-modeling tool when the business category is closed. They communicate architectural intent better than comments or package conventions.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need Use sealed type? Reason
Closed domain outcomes Yes Exhaustive handling
Plugin extension point No External extension required
Internal error taxonomy Yes Controlled variants
Public SPI Carefully May block consumers
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Approach Extension model Best use
final class No extension Single implementation
Open interface Anyone extends Plugin/API contracts
Sealed interface Known implementors Closed polymorphic model
Enum Fixed constants Simple closed values
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Sealing plugin interfaces, forgetting subtype modifiers, exposing sealed hierarchies without serialization strategy, and using sealed classes where an enum is enough are common mistakes.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. What must permitted subclasses declare?
  2. How do sealed classes support exhaustive switch handling?
  3. When is an enum better than a sealed hierarchy?
  4. What are API compatibility risks of adding a subtype?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • Sealed types restrict inheritance.
  • Subtypes must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.
  • Use sealed types for closed polymorphic models.
  • Public sealed APIs require versioning care.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Controlled inheritance
JVM Permitted subclass verification
Performance Mostly modeling benefit
Architecture Strong for closed domain variants

Practice — Lesson 19

Model a sealed OrderCommandResult hierarchy with success, validation failure, conflict, and async accepted variants. Add a switch that maps each variant to an HTTP response.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

The Java Platform Module System, or JPMS, organizes code into named modules with explicit dependencies and exported packages. It gives stronger encapsulation than packages alone.

module com.acme.orders
  requires com.acme.common
  exports com.acme.orders.api
Part 2

History

JPMS shipped in Java 9 through Project Jigsaw. It modularized the JDK itself and introduced module-info.java for application and library modules.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Classpath-based Java has weak boundaries. Any public class on the classpath can be accessed, dependency conflicts are hard to diagnose, and large runtimes include unnecessary JDK modules.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

JPMS provides reliable configuration, strong encapsulation, smaller runtime images, explicit dependency graphs, and better maintainability for large systems.

Part 5

Internal Working

A module descriptor declares module name, required modules, exported packages, opened packages, provided services, and consumed services. The module graph is resolved at launch or layer creation.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

The JVM has a module layer containing resolved modules. Access checks consider both Java visibility and module exports/opens.

Part 7

Memory Layout

Modules do not alter object layout. They add runtime metadata about readable modules, exported packages, and reflective openness.

Boot Layer
  java.base
  java.sql
  com.acme.orders
      exports api
      hides internal
Part 8

Execution Flow

  1. Module descriptors are discovered.
  2. Resolver builds dependency graph.
  3. JVM creates a module layer.
  4. Classes load within modules.
  5. Access checks enforce exports and opens.
Part 9

Performance Analysis

JPMS can improve startup and footprint when paired with jlink custom runtimes. It may add build and migration complexity for reflection-heavy frameworks.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Module resolution is graph-based and occurs at startup or layer creation. Normal method execution complexity is unchanged after resolution.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Module descriptors and graph metadata add small overhead. Custom runtime images can reduce disk and memory footprint by excluding unused modules.

Part 12

Code Examples

module com.acme.orders {
    requires java.sql;
    requires com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;

    exports com.acme.orders.api;
    opens com.acme.orders.api to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

JPMS is common in platform libraries, desktop applications, command-line tools, and JDK runtime image optimization. Many Spring Boot services still use the classpath because ecosystem reflection and plugins are simpler there.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring Boot can run with JPMS, but many applications remain non-modular. Reflection-heavy features may require opens directives for Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, and validation frameworks.

module com.acme.orders {
    requires spring.boot;
    requires spring.boot.autoconfigure;
    requires spring.context;

    opens com.acme.orders.web to spring.core, spring.beans, spring.context;
}
Part 15

Microservice Usage

JPMS can be useful for large service codebases and shared libraries, but containers already isolate deployments. The highest value is compile-time and runtime boundary enforcement inside the service.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Adopt JPMS when strong module boundaries, custom runtimes, or platform-level libraries justify the migration cost. Do not force JPMS into every Spring microservice unless the organization can maintain module descriptors well.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Need JPMS fit Reason
Shared platform library Strong Enforced exported API
Simple Spring Boot service Mixed Added descriptor burden
Custom runtime image Strong jlink benefits
Plugin-heavy app Careful Dynamic loading complexity
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Aspect Classpath Module path
Dependency declaration Implicit Explicit requires
Public access Any public class Only exported packages
Reflection Broadly permissive Requires opens
Runtime image Full JDK commonly Can use jlink
Part 19

Common Mistakes

Exporting every package, confusing exports with opens, ignoring automatic module names, migrating reflection-heavy applications without a plan, and treating JPMS as a replacement for service boundaries are common mistakes.

Part 20

Interview Questions

  1. What problem does JPMS solve beyond packages?
  2. What is the difference between exports and opens?
  3. Why does reflection behave differently with modules?
  4. When would you use jlink?
Part 21

Revision Sheet

  • JPMS adds explicit module dependencies.
  • exports is for compile/runtime public API access.
  • opens is for deep reflection.
  • Modules strengthen boundaries but add migration cost.
Part 22

Summary Table

Topic Key takeaway
Purpose Strong modular boundaries
JVM Module layers and access checks
Performance Enables smaller runtime images
Architecture Useful when boundary enforcement pays off

Practice — Lesson 20

Draft a module-info.java for an orders library. Export only API packages, open DTO packages only to Jackson, and explain whether the same strategy is worth applying to a Spring Boot microservice.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

The Java Collection Framework is a unified set of interfaces, implementations, algorithms, and conventions for storing groups of objects.

Core families:

Family Main Interfaces Typical Implementations Primary Use
Collection List, Set, Queue, Deque ArrayList, HashSet, ArrayDeque Element groups
Map Map, ConcurrentMap, NavigableMap HashMap, ConcurrentHashMap, TreeMap Key-value lookup
Algorithms Collections, Arrays Static utilities Sorting, searching, wrappers 
Iterable
  |
Collection
  |-- List
  |-- Set
  |-- Queue
      |-- Deque

Map   // separate root, not a Collection
Part 2

History

Before Java 1.2, Java had Vector, Stack, Hashtable, Dictionary, and Enumeration. They were inconsistent, synchronized by default, and lacked a common abstraction.

Java 1.2 introduced the Collection Framework with interfaces, fail-fast iterators, optional operations, and reusable algorithms. Later releases added generics, concurrent collections, navigable collections, streams, immutable factories, and sequenced collections.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Large systems need a standard way to represent ordered data, unique data, queues, graphs, indexes, caches, and snapshots. Without common contracts, every library invents incompatible containers and algorithm APIs.

The framework solves:

Problem Framework Answer
Different container APIs Common interfaces
Unsafe casts Generics
Inefficient algorithm rewrites Utility algorithms
Multi-threaded access Concurrent implementations
API flexibility Program to interfaces
Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides collections because object grouping is foundational to almost every application layer: controllers receive lists, repositories return pages, services build maps, caches index records, and infrastructure queues work.

Architecturally, collections are Java's standard vocabulary for data shape.

Part 5

Internal Working

The framework separates contract from storage strategy.

Interface contract
  List: order + positional access
  Set: uniqueness
  Queue: processing order
  Map: key lookup

Implementation strategy
  ArrayList: resizable array
  LinkedList: node chain
  HashMap: hash table + tree bins
  TreeMap: red-black tree

This separation lets APIs expose List<Order> while callers choose ArrayList, immutable lists, or framework-provided views.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Collections are normal heap objects. Interfaces compile to invokeinterface; concrete calls may be optimized by the JIT with profiling, inlining, and escape analysis.

Important JVM realities:

JVM Concern Impact
Object headers Node-based collections are memory-heavy
References Collections store references, not inline objects
Generics erasure Runtime mostly sees Object
JIT profiling Hot collection calls can inline
GC roots Long-lived collections retain whole object graphs
Part 7

Memory Layout

Example ArrayList<User>:

ArrayList object
  elementData ---> Object[] array
                   [ref0][ref1][ref2][null]
                     |     |     |
                    User  User  User

Example HashMap<String, User>:

HashMap
  table ---> Node[] buckets
              [0] -> Node(key, value, hash, next)
              [1] -> null
              [2] -> Node -> Node

The collection owns container structures, not the domain objects themselves.

Part 8

Execution Flow

Typical service flow:

List<Order> orders = orderRepository.findRecent(customerId);
Map<OrderStatus, List<Order>> byStatus = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status));
Set<String> productIds = orders.stream()
    .map(Order::productId)
    .collect(Collectors.toSet());

Execution moves from ordered retrieval to indexed grouping to unique identifier extraction.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Performance comes from matching access pattern to implementation.

Access Pattern Good Choice Poor Choice
Append and index ArrayList LinkedList
Unique membership HashSet ArrayList.contains
Sorted traversal TreeSet Sort every request
Key lookup HashMap Linear scans
Concurrent counters ConcurrentHashMap synchronized HashMap

Structure Space Cost Notes

Part 12

Code Examples

public final class CollectionSelection {
    public List<String> preserveOrder(Collection<String> input) {
        return new ArrayList<>(input);
    }

    public Set<String> uniqueIds(Collection<String> input) {
        return new HashSet<>(input);
    }

    public Map<String, Long> frequency(Collection<String> input) {
        Map<String, Long> result = new HashMap<>();
        for (String value : input) {
            result.merge(value, 1L, Long::sum);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

List represents an ordered sequence that permits duplicates and positional access.

index:   0      1      2      3
list: [order1][order2][order2][order3]

Main implementations:

Implementation Storage Best For
ArrayList Resizable array Reads, appends, indexed access
LinkedList Doubly linked nodes Queue-like use, rare niche cases
CopyOnWriteArrayList Snapshot array copies Small, read-heavy concurrent lists
Immutable lists Fixed array Safe API responses and configs
Part 2

History

Vector existed before the framework and synchronized every method. ArrayList arrived in Java 1.2 as the unsynchronized general-purpose replacement. Generics made lists type-safe, Java 8 integrated streams, Java 9 added factory methods, and newer Java releases improved immutable and sequenced collection APIs.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Applications frequently need ordered duplicates: invoice lines, validation messages, search results, route steps, batch records, and rule chains.

List solves:

Need Example
Stable order API response ordering
Duplicates Multiple order lines for same SKU
Positional access Pagination windows
Iteration Batch processing
Bulk operations addAll, sort, replaceAll
Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides List because sequence is one of the most common data shapes in business software. It allows libraries to expose ordered data without committing callers to a concrete storage model.

Use the interface in APIs:

public List<OrderDto> findOrders(String customerId) {
    return List.copyOf(queryOrders(customerId));
}
Part 5

Internal Working

ArrayList stores elements in an Object[] and grows when capacity is exceeded.

ArrayList
  size = 3
  elementData -> [A][B][C][null][null]

LinkedList stores each element in a node.

first -> [prev null | A | next] <-> [prev | B | next] <-> [prev | C | null]

Array-backed lists usually win due to cache locality and lower object overhead.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Generics are erased, so List<Order> is backed by references in an Object[]. The compiler inserts casts at read sites. HotSpot can inline common list methods when the receiver type is stable.

JVM-level concerns:

Concern Impact
Bounds checks Often optimized in loops
Reference arrays Compact compared with nodes
Growth copies System.arraycopy is highly optimized
Escape analysis Short-lived lists may be optimized
GC retention Removing elements must clear references
Part 7

Memory Layout

ArrayList:

ArrayList object
  size: 3
  elementData ----+
                 v
Object[]:     [ref][ref][ref][null]
                |    |    |
              Order Order Order

LinkedList:

LinkedList
  first -> Node -> Node -> Node
  last --------------------^

Each Node = object header + item ref + prev ref + next ref
Part 8

Execution Flow

List<Order> orders = repository.findByCustomerId(customerId);
orders.sort(Comparator.comparing(Order::createdAt).reversed());

for (Order order : orders) {
    publisher.publish(order);
}

Flow: retrieve ordered records, sort in memory, iterate once. For very large result sets, prefer database sorting and streaming windows.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Operation ArrayList LinkedList
Append Amortized O(1) O(1)
Get by index O(1) O(n)
Insert middle O(n) shift O(n) traversal + O(1) link
Remove middle O(n) shift O(n) traversal + O(1) link
Iterate Fast Slower due to pointer chasing

LinkedList is rarely the correct default in modern JVM services.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Method Complexity Notes
get(i) O(1) for ArrayList O(n) for LinkedList
add(e) Amortized O(1) Occasional resize
add(i, e) O(n) Shifts or traversal
contains(e) O(n) Uses equals
sort(c) O(n log n) TimSort
subList O(1) view creation Backed by original
Part 11

Space Complexity

List Type Space
ArrayList O(n) plus spare capacity
LinkedList O(n) plus node objects
CopyOnWriteArrayList O(n) per snapshot copy during writes
Immutable list O(n), compact for fixed data

Oversized lists increase heap retention; under-sized lists can trigger repeated copies.

Part 12

Code Examples

public final class ListExamples {
    public List<String> normalize(List<String> names) {
        return names.stream()
            .filter(Objects::nonNull)
            .map(String::trim)
            .filter(name -> !name.isEmpty())
            .toList();
    }

    public List<Order> newestFirst(Collection<Order> orders) {
        List<Order> copy = new ArrayList<>(orders);
        copy.sort(Comparator.comparing(Order::createdAt).reversed());
        return List.copyOf(copy);
    }
}

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Set is a collection that does not allow duplicate elements. Duplicate detection depends on equals and, for hash-based sets, hashCode.

input:  [A][B][A][C]
set:    [A][B][C]

Common implementations:

Implementation Ordering Mechanism
HashSet None Hash table
LinkedHashSet Insertion order Hash table + linked order
TreeSet Sorted Red-black tree
EnumSet Enum natural order Bit vector
Concurrent set Usually none ConcurrentHashMap keys
Part 2

History

Set entered Java with the 1.2 Collection Framework. Generics made membership type-safe, EnumSet added compact enum handling, concurrent map-backed sets became common, and immutable set factories made safe publication easier.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Many domains require uniqueness: user roles, visited IDs, processed message IDs, feature flags, blocked countries, and permissions.

Without Set, systems often use lists and manual checks, causing duplicate bugs and O(n) membership scans.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides Set to express uniqueness as a first-class contract. That contract is stronger and clearer than "a list we promise not to duplicate."

record UserProfile(String id, Set<String> roles) {}

The type itself tells consumers that duplicate roles are meaningless.

Part 5

Internal Working

HashSet is backed by HashMap; elements are stored as map keys with a dummy value.

HashSet
  map -> HashMap
           key = element
           value = PRESENT

TreeSet is backed by TreeMap; ordering comes from natural ordering or a comparator.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

A HashSet allocation creates a set object and an internal HashMap. Each element becomes a key reference in a hash table node or tree bin.

JVM details:

Detail Effect
Hash collisions More equality checks
Tree bins Worst-case lookup improves after threshold
Mutable keys Can make elements unreachable by lookup
EnumSet bit vector Very compact and fast
JIT inlining Hot contains can optimize well
Part 7

Memory Layout

HashSet:

HashSet
  HashMap
    table -> [bucket0][bucket1][bucket2]
                         |
                       Node
                      key -> Role("ADMIN")
                    value -> PRESENT

EnumSet:

EnumSet permissions
  bits: 00010110
        READ WRITE APPROVE flags encoded by bit position
Part 8

Execution Flow

Set<String> requestedIds = new HashSet<>(request.productIds());
List<Product> products = repository.findAllById(requestedIds);

if (products.size() != requestedIds.size()) {
    throw new MissingProductException();
}

The set removes duplicates before the repository call and makes size comparison meaningful.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Set Type Contains Add Iteration Order Notes
HashSet O(1) avg O(1) avg Undefined Default
LinkedHashSet O(1) avg O(1) avg Insertion Deterministic
TreeSet O(log n) O(log n) Sorted Range queries
EnumSet O(1) O(1) Enum order Best for enums
Part 10

Time Complexity

Operation HashSet LinkedHashSet TreeSet EnumSet
add O(1) avg O(1) avg O(log n) O(1)
contains O(1) avg O(1) avg O(log n) O(1)
remove O(1) avg O(1) avg O(log n) O(1)
Iterate O(n + capacity) O(n) O(n) O(enum constants)
Part 11

Space Complexity

Set Type Space Cost
HashSet O(n + buckets)
LinkedHashSet O(n + buckets + order links)
TreeSet O(n) nodes
EnumSet O(1) or O(k words)
Concurrent key set O(n + concurrent map metadata)
Part 12

Code Examples

public final class RoleService {
    public Set<Role> normalizeRoles(Collection<Role> roles) {
        EnumSet<Role> normalized = EnumSet.noneOf(Role.class);
        normalized.addAll(roles);
        normalized.remove(Role.DEPRECATED);
        return Set.copyOf(normalized);
    }

    public boolean hasAnyRole(Set<Role> userRoles, Set<Role> required) {
        return required.stream().anyMatch(userRoles::contains);
    }
}

Real Production Examples

Scenario Set Choice

Preserve upload order while deduping LinkedHashSet<String>

Concurrent active sessions ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()

@PostMapping("/products/quote")

Microservice set patterns:

Pattern Set Role

Bound in-memory sets; unbounded idempotency sets should move to Redis, database, or compact probabilistic structures.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Sets encode invariants. If duplicates are impossible by design, Set is better than validating a List everywhere.

Tradeoffs:

Decision Tradeoff
HashSet vs LinkedHashSet Speed vs deterministic output
HashSet vs TreeSet Lookup speed vs sorted/range access
In-memory set vs external store Latency vs durability
Exact set vs Bloom filter Correctness vs memory
Mutable set vs immutable set Flexibility vs invariant safety

Decision Matrix

Requirement Recommended Set
Fast uniqueness HashSet
Deterministic insertion order LinkedHashSet
Sorted unique values TreeSet
Enum flags EnumSet
Concurrent add/remove ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()
Public response Set.copyOf

Feature HashSet LinkedHashSet TreeSet EnumSet
Allows null One One Depends comparator No
Sorted No No Yes Enum order
Preserves insertion No Yes No No
Memory Medium Higher Higher Very low
Best use Membership Stable dedupe Ranges Enum flags

Assuming HashSet order Flaky tests and APIs
Using TreeSet with inconsistent comparator Lost elements
Using Set when duplicates are meaningful Data loss

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Queue models elements waiting to be processed. Deque extends that idea to both ends, supporting FIFO, LIFO, and double-ended workflows.

Queue FIFO:
offer -> [A][B][C] -> poll returns A

Deque:
addFirst <-> [A][B][C] <-> addLast
Interface Core Idea Common Implementation
Queue Process in policy order ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue
Deque Add/remove both ends ArrayDeque
BlockingQueue Thread coordination ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue
Part 2

History

Early Java used Vector/Stack and ad hoc lists for queue behavior. Java 5 added Queue, Deque, and java.util.concurrent queues, enabling producer-consumer patterns without hand-written wait/notify code.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Systems need to hold work before processing: retries, BFS traversal, rate-limited jobs, async handoff, priority scheduling, and recent-item buffers.

Queues solve:

Problem Queue Feature
Decouple producers and consumers Buffering
Process oldest first FIFO
Process highest priority first Priority queue
Coordinate threads Blocking queues
Model stack without legacy Stack Deque.push/pop
Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides queue abstractions because processing order is different from storage order. A List can hold work, but a Queue makes the processing contract explicit.

Queue<Job> jobs = new ArrayDeque<>();
jobs.offer(new Job("email"));
Job next = jobs.poll();
Part 5

Internal Working

ArrayDeque uses a circular array.

elements: [D][E][ ][ ][A][B][C]
                  ^       ^
                 tail    head

PriorityQueue uses a binary heap.

        1
      /   \
     4     3
    / \
   9   7

The smallest or comparator-highest element is at the heap root.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Queue implementations are heap objects with arrays or nodes. Blocking queues use locks, conditions, volatile fields, or compare-and-swap depending on implementation.

Implementation JVM Mechanism
ArrayDeque Plain object array
PriorityQueue Plain object array heap
ArrayBlockingQueue Fixed array + lock conditions
LinkedBlockingQueue Nodes + separate put/take locks
ConcurrentLinkedQueue Lock-free CAS linked nodes
Part 7

Memory Layout

ArrayDeque:

ArrayDeque
  head = 5
  tail = 2
  elements -> [E][F][null][null][null][A][B][C][D]

LinkedBlockingQueue:

head -> Node(null) -> Node(task1) -> Node(task2) <- tail

Node queues cost more memory but can grow without copying.

Part 8

Execution Flow

Deque<String> retryStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
retryStack.addLast("job-1");
retryStack.addLast("job-2");

while (!retryStack.isEmpty()) {
    String jobId = retryStack.removeFirst();
    process(jobId);
}

Use offer/poll/peek when absence is normal; use add/remove/element when absence indicates a bug.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Operation ArrayDeque LinkedList as Deque PriorityQueue
Add head/tail Amortized O(1) O(1) N/A
Remove head/tail O(1) O(1) N/A
Peek best N/A N/A O(1)
Add priority item N/A N/A O(log n)
Remove best N/A N/A O(log n)
Part 10

Time Complexity

Method Complexity Notes
offer on ArrayDeque Amortized O(1) May resize
poll on ArrayDeque O(1) Clears reference
push/pop on ArrayDeque O(1) Stack behavior
PriorityQueue.offer O(log n) Heap up
PriorityQueue.poll O(log n) Heap down
contains O(n) Avoid for membership
Part 11

Space Complexity

Queue Type Space
ArrayDeque O(n) plus spare capacity
PriorityQueue O(n) array
LinkedBlockingQueue O(n) nodes
ArrayBlockingQueue O(capacity) fixed
ConcurrentLinkedQueue O(n) nodes

Bounded queues are often safer in services because unbounded queues hide overload until the heap fails.

Part 12

Code Examples

public final class QueueExamples {
    public List<String> bfs(Map<String, List<String>> graph, String start) {
        Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>();
        Queue<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        List<String> order = new ArrayList<>();

        visited.add(start);
        queue.offer(start);

        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            String node = queue.poll();
            order.add(node);
            for (String next : graph.getOrDefault(node, List.of())) {
                if (visited.add(next)) {
                    queue.offer(next);
                }
            }
        }
        return order;
    }
}
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Scenario Queue Choice
Local BFS traversal ArrayDeque
In-memory retry buffer Bounded ArrayBlockingQueue
Priority job order PriorityQueue
Many producer/consumer threads LinkedBlockingQueue
Lock-free event handoff ConcurrentLinkedQueue
Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

@Component
class LocalEmailBuffer {
    private final BlockingQueue<EmailCommand> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10_000);

    boolean enqueue(EmailCommand command) {
        return queue.offer(command);
    }

    EmailCommand take() throws InterruptedException {
        return queue.take();
    }
}

In Spring services, local queues should be bounded and observable.

Part 15

Microservice Usage

Microservice queue design:

Concern Guidance
Back-pressure Prefer bounded queues
Durability Use Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, or DB outbox
Ordering Define partition or queue ordering
Retries Separate immediate retry from delayed retry
Shutdown Drain or reject gracefully

In-memory queues are not durable; do not use them as message brokers.

Part 16

Architect Perspective

Queue design is capacity design.

Decision Tradeoff
Bounded vs unbounded Fail fast vs heap risk
In-memory vs broker Low latency vs durability
FIFO vs priority Fairness vs business urgency
Blocking vs non-blocking Simpler coordination vs explicit polling
Local retry vs distributed retry Simplicity vs reliability
Part 17

Decision Matrix

Requirement Choice
General FIFO/LIFO ArrayDeque
Stack replacement ArrayDeque
Priority processing PriorityQueue
Thread handoff with bounds ArrayBlockingQueue
Producer-consumer with variable load LinkedBlockingQueue with capacity
Durable async workflow External broker

Thread-safe No No Yes Yes
Bounded No No Yes No
Ordering FIFO/LIFO Priority FIFO FIFO
Blocking ops No No Yes No
Nulls No No No No

Mistake Consequence
Using Stack Legacy synchronized API
Using unbounded queues in services Memory failure under overload
Expecting PriorityQueue iteration to be sorted Incorrect output

Using local queues for durable jobs Data loss on restart

Part 1

Concept

Map stores associations from unique keys to values. It is not a subtype of Collection because it stores pairs rather than individual elements.

customerId -> Customer
sku        -> Price
tenantId   -> FeatureConfig
Implementation Ordering Main Use
HashMap Undefined Fast lookup
LinkedHashMap Insertion/access Deterministic output, LRU
TreeMap Sorted keys Range queries
EnumMap Enum key order Compact enum keyed maps
ConcurrentHashMap Undefined Concurrent access
Part 2

History

Before the Collection Framework, Java used Hashtable and Dictionary. Java 1.2 introduced Map and HashMap; Java 5 added ConcurrentHashMap; Java 8 added functional methods such as computeIfAbsent and merge; Java 9 added immutable factories.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Applications need fast lookup and grouping: user by ID, price by SKU, orders by status, config by tenant, and locks by resource.

Without maps, code degrades into repeated list scans, fragile parallel arrays, or custom indexes.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides Map because key-based access is a core data structure independent of relational databases or caches.

Map<String, Product> bySku = products.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Product::sku, Function.identity()));

The key type represents the lookup contract.

Part 5

Internal Working

HashMap uses an array of buckets. Each bucket holds nodes, and heavily collided buckets can become tree bins.

table
 [0] null
 [1] Node(k1,v1) -> Node(k2,v2)
 [2] Node(k3,v3)

Index selection is based on the spread hash and table length.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Keys and values are object references. Hash computation invokes user code, often hashCode. Equality invokes equals. Hot paths can be inlined, but poor key design still dominates performance.

JVM Detail Impact
Node allocations Memory and GC pressure
Resizing Rehash and table copy
Tree bins Better collision worst case
Final immutable keys Safer hash behavior
Concurrent map bins CAS and synchronization in hot buckets
Part 7

Memory Layout

HashMap
  size = 3
  threshold = 12
  table -> Node[]
             [0] -> null
             [1] -> Node(hash, keyRef, valueRef, next)
                         keyRef -> "sku-1"
                         valueRef -> Product

EnumMap uses an array indexed by enum ordinal:

enum ordinal: NEW=0 PAID=1 SHIPPED=2
values:      [cfg0][cfg1][cfg2]
Part 8

Execution Flow

Map<String, Order> byId = new HashMap<>(orders.size() * 2);
for (Order order : orders) {
    Order previous = byId.put(order.id(), order);
    if (previous != null) {
        throw new DuplicateOrderException(order.id());
    }
}

Flow: size for expected load, insert by stable key, detect duplicates at insertion time.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

Map performance depends on key quality, sizing, mutation, and access pattern.

Issue Result
Poor hash distribution Long bucket chains
Mutable key fields Missing entries
Under-sizing Repeated resize
Over-sizing Wasted memory and slower iteration
Need sorted ranges HashMap cannot help
Part 10

Time Complexity

Operation HashMap LinkedHashMap TreeMap EnumMap
put O(1) avg O(1) avg O(log n) O(1)
get O(1) avg O(1) avg O(log n) O(1)
remove O(1) avg O(1) avg O(log n) O(1)
Iterate O(capacity + n) O(n) O(n) sorted O(enum size)
Range query No No O(log n + k) No
Part 11

Space Complexity

Map Type Space
HashMap O(n + buckets)
LinkedHashMap O(n + buckets + links)
TreeMap O(n) tree nodes
EnumMap O(enum constants)
ConcurrentHashMap O(n + bins + concurrency metadata)
Part 12

Code Examples

public final class MapExamples {
    public Map<OrderStatus, Long> countByStatus(List<Order> orders) {
        Map<OrderStatus, Long> counts = new EnumMap<>(OrderStatus.class);
        for (Order order : orders) {
            counts.merge(order.status(), 1L, Long::sum);
        }
        return Map.copyOf(counts);
    }

    public Map<String, List<Order>> groupByCustomer(List<Order> orders) {
        Map<String, List<Order>> result = new HashMap<>();
        for (Order order : orders) {
            result.computeIfAbsent(order.customerId(), ignored -> new ArrayList<>()).add(order);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Real Production Examples

Scenario Map Choice
Request DTO by ID HashMap<String, Dto>
Ordered JSON object output LinkedHashMap
LRU local cache Access-order LinkedHashMap
Price ranges by date TreeMap<LocalDate, Price>
Status configuration EnumMap<Status, Config>
Shared in-memory registry ConcurrentHashMap
Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

@Service
class PaymentRouter {
    private final Map<String, PaymentClient> clientsByProvider;

    PaymentRouter(List<PaymentClient> clients) {
        this.clientsByProvider = clients.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(PaymentClient::provider, Function.identity()));
    }

    PaymentClient client(String provider) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(clientsByProvider.get(provider))
            .orElseThrow(() -> new UnknownProviderException(provider));
    }
}

Spring can inject a Map<String, Bean> by bean name, but explicit keys are usually clearer.

Maps are often the first in-memory cache; architecture must define invalidation.

Decision Tradeoff
