Commands: jstack <pid>, jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, and java -Xss512k for sizing experiments.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Thread pools in Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow, schedulers, and async executors multiply stack reservations. Review pool sizes before increasing pod memory.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Blocking microservices with large worker pools can waste memory on stacks. Reactive or virtual-thread models shift the tradeoff but still require profiling.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architect Perspective

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Lower -Xss only after recursion and native libraries are understood. Reduce thread counts before shrinking stack aggressively.

Part 1

Concept

Metaspace is native memory used primarily for class metadata. It grows and shrinks with class loading and class unloading, not with ordinary object allocation.

JVM Process RSS
+-- Java Heap: objects, arrays, TLABs
+-- Thread Stacks: frames, locals, operand stacks
+-- Metaspace: class metadata
+-- Code Cache: compiled methods
+-- Native/Direct: buffers, libc, GC structures
Part 2

History

Java 8 replaced fixed-size PermGen with metaspace to reduce tuning pain, but classloader leaks and unlimited native growth remained operational risks.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Metaspace OOM usually means too many loaded classes, dynamic proxy generation, repeated classloader creation, disabled class unloading, or a framework/plugin leak.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java stores class metadata outside the heap so metadata management can follow classloader lifetimes and avoid squeezing application objects in the heap.

Part 5

Internal Working

A classloader defines classes; metadata is allocated in metaspace chunks; unloading occurs only when the classloader and all its classes are unreachable and a GC performs unloading.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot manages metaspace with native virtual memory spaces and chunks. MaxMetaspaceSize caps growth; class unloading is collector-dependent but broadly supported.

java -Xlog:class+load=info,class+unload=info -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats
jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace
Part 7

Memory Layout

Metaspace holds Klass structures, method metadata, constant pools, annotations, vtables, itables, and reflection-supporting metadata. Class mirrors are ordinary heap objects.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Load class -> allocate metadata -> execute application -> classloader becomes unreachable -> GC detects unloadable classes -> metaspace chunks reclaimed or reused.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For metaspace, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

Part 12

Code Examples

java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -Xlog:metaspace=info,class+load=info -jar app.jar

Diagnostic example:

java -Xlog:class+load=info,class+unload=info -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats
jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Use jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace, jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats, jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram, and -Xlog:class+unload=info.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring creates proxies and scans many classes. Devtools restart classloaders, plugin systems, and dynamic script engines need special leak attention.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Long-lived microservices rarely unload classes in normal operation, so steady metaspace growth after startup is suspicious and worth alerting.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architect Perspective

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Set MaxMetaspaceSize as a guardrail, but fix leaks rather than hiding them. Keep dynamic class generation bounded.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Garbage collection automatically identifies unreachable objects, reclaims memory, and often compacts or relocates live data to maintain allocation efficiency.

GC Cycle
Roots -> Mark Live Objects -> Select Regions/Spaces -> Evacuate or Sweep -> Update References
          ^                         |                      |
          +------- concurrent phases may overlap application threads -------+
Part 2

History

Java evolved from stop-the-world collectors to generational, parallel, regional, and concurrent low-latency collectors as heaps and latency expectations grew.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Bad GC behavior appears as pauses, CPU burn, allocation stalls, promotion failures, humongous fragmentation, finalizer/reference delays, and OOM despite apparent free memory.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides GC to remove manual free errors, centralize memory safety, and let runtimes optimize allocation and reclamation according to workload.

Part 5

Internal Working

Collectors find roots from stacks, statics, JNI handles, and registers; trace reachable objects; reclaim unreachable memory; and coordinate application threads with barriers and safepoints.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot offers Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah depending on JDK/build. Unified logging exposes phases with -Xlog:gc*.

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 7

Memory Layout

GC metadata includes card tables, remembered sets, mark bitmaps, forwarding pointers, evacuation buffers, and per-thread allocation buffers.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Allocation pressure -> young or old collection trigger -> roots scanned -> live objects marked/copied/compacted -> references processed -> application resumes or continues concurrently.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For garbage collection, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

Part 12

Code Examples

jcmd <pid> GC.run
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=gc settings=profile filename=/tmp/gc.jfr

Diagnostic example:

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Start with -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags and inspect with GCViewer, GCeasy, or JDK Mission Control.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring services with large JSON payloads, caches, Hibernate graphs, and actuator snapshots can create allocation bursts that dominate GC.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

GC tuning must consider pod CPU limits. A collector starved of CPU can miss latency goals even with enough memory.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architect Perspective

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Pick collector by SLO: Parallel for throughput, G1 as balanced default, ZGC/Shenandoah for low latency and large heaps.

Strict tail latency ZGC/Shenandoah evaluation Throughput-only tuning Concurrent collectors reduce long pauses
Memory-dense container MaxRAMPercentage, direct-memory cap, thread control -Xmx equal to limit Prevents RSS OOMKill
Unknown incident jcmd, JFR, dumps, GC logs Blind restart Preserves root-cause evidence

ZGC/Shenandoah Very low pauses More CPU/headroom and version sensitivity Large heaps and strict p99/p999
Parallel GC High throughput Longer pauses Batch and offline jobs
JFR/async-profiler Production insight Needs process and storage controls Incident and optimization work
Part 19

Common Mistakes

  • Tuning flags without GC logs, JFR, or load-test evidence.
  • Ignoring non-heap memory in Kubernetes.
  • Treating average latency as success while p99 violates the SLO.
  • Taking heap dumps on overloaded nodes without planning disk and pause impact.
  • Changing multiple JVM variables at once and losing causality.

Part 1

Concept

GC algorithms are the strategies collectors use: mark-sweep, mark-compact, copying, generational collection, region evacuation, and concurrent tracing.

GC Cycle
Roots -> Mark Live Objects -> Select Regions/Spaces -> Evacuate or Sweep -> Update References
          ^                         |                      |
          +------- concurrent phases may overlap application threads -------+
Part 2

History

Simple mark-sweep gave way to copying young collectors, parallel compaction, CMS, G1 regions, and modern concurrent compacting designs.

Part 3

Problem Statement

No algorithm wins everywhere. The wrong choice can trade low allocation cost for fragmentation, or low pauses for higher CPU and memory overhead.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides multiple algorithms because workloads differ by live-set size, allocation rate, latency budget, CPU headroom, object lifetime, and heap scale.

Part 5

Internal Working

Marking traces live objects; sweeping frees dead objects; copying evacuates live objects to new space; compaction removes fragmentation; concurrency overlaps GC with application work.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot collectors compose algorithms: Parallel uses generational copying and compaction; G1 uses regional evacuation and concurrent marking; ZGC/Shenandoah use concurrent relocation barriers.

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 7

Memory Layout

Algorithms maintain mark bits, forwarding metadata, remembered sets, evacuation spaces, free lists, and region state. Overhead is part of capacity planning.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Trigger -> choose collection set or space -> scan roots -> mark/copy/compact -> update references -> return memory to allocation paths.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For gc algorithms, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

  java -XX:+$gc -Xlog:gc*:file=gc-$gc.log -jar app.jar
done

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 13

Compare with -XX:+UseParallelGC, -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseZGC, and -XX:+UseShenandoahGC on the same workload and GC log format.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Framework allocation patterns are often short-lived, which favors generational collection. Large caches and session-like state increase old-generation pressure.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

For services, algorithm choice should be validated with representative traffic, pod CPU limits, and real payload distributions rather than synthetic averages.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Favor G1 unless evidence suggests otherwise; choose ZGC/Shenandoah for strict tail-latency; choose Parallel for batch throughput.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

G1GC is a regional, mostly concurrent collector designed to balance throughput and predictable pauses by collecting selected heap regions first.

GC Cycle
Roots -> Mark Live Objects -> Select Regions/Spaces -> Evacuate or Sweep -> Update References
          ^                         |                      |
          +------- concurrent phases may overlap application threads -------+
Part 2

History

G1 replaced CMS as the default server collector because it handles fragmentation better, supports large heaps, and exposes pause-goal ergonomics.

Part 3

Problem Statement

G1 issues include humongous allocation fragmentation, remembered-set overhead, evacuation failures, mixed-GC inefficiency, and pause goals that cannot be met with limited CPU.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides G1 to give most server applications a balanced default without requiring deep generation sizing and compaction tuning.

Part 5

Internal Working

The heap is split into regions. Young collections evacuate Eden/survivor regions. Concurrent marking identifies old-region liveness. Mixed collections reclaim selected old regions with high garbage value.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot tracks remembered sets for cross-region references, uses SATB marking, predicts pause cost, and chooses collection sets to target MaxGCPauseMillis.

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 7

Memory Layout

G1 heap regions are commonly 1-32 MB. Humongous objects larger than half a region occupy contiguous humongous regions and can fragment the heap.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Young GC -> concurrent mark starts near IHOP -> remark -> cleanup -> mixed GCs reclaim old regions -> cycle repeats as occupancy changes.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For g1gc, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

Part 12

Code Examples

java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms2g -Xmx2g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
  -Xlog:gc*,gc+heap=debug,gc+ergo=trace:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags \
  -jar service.jar

Diagnostic example:

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Flags: -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200, -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45, -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m, -Xlog:gc+ergo=debug.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

G1 is a strong default for Spring Boot services. Watch large response buffers, caches, and byte arrays that become humongous allocations.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

In Kubernetes, G1 needs CPU during concurrent marking. Tight CPU limits can cause marking to lag and trigger Full GC.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Tune G1 only after reading logs: adjust heap first, then pause target, IHOP, region size, and humongous allocation behavior.

Part 1

Concept

ZGC and Shenandoah are low-latency collectors that perform most marking, relocation, and reference processing concurrently with application threads.

GC Cycle
Roots -> Mark Live Objects -> Select Regions/Spaces -> Evacuate or Sweep -> Update References
          ^                         |                      |
          +------- concurrent phases may overlap application threads -------+
Part 2

History

They emerged to support large heaps and strict tail-latency targets that regional stop-the-world collectors struggled to meet.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Low-latency collectors reduce pauses but may cost more CPU, require newer JDKs, expose different tuning surfaces, and need operational confidence before broad rollout.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides these collectors so services with large live sets can meet latency SLOs without splitting heaps artificially or accepting long compaction pauses.

Part 5

Internal Working

ZGC uses colored pointers and load barriers; Shenandoah uses barriers and forwarding metadata. Both relocate objects concurrently and keep application references correct.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot ZGC is production-ready on modern JDKs. Shenandoah availability depends on distribution/build. Generational ZGC in newer JDKs improves handling of short-lived allocations.

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 7

Memory Layout

Expect extra headroom for concurrent work, relocation sets, marking metadata, and allocation spikes while GC catches up. Low pause does not mean zero memory overhead.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Concurrent mark -> brief root/safepoint phases -> concurrent relocation planning -> concurrent object relocation -> barriers repair or redirect references -> repeat before allocation stalls.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For zgc & shenandoah, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

  -Xlog:gc*:file=zgc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar service.jar

Part 13

Real Production Examples

Flags: -XX:+UseZGC, -XX:+ZGenerational, -XX:+UseShenandoahGC, -Xlog:gc*,gc+reloc=debug, and jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Low-latency collectors help APIs with strict p99/p999 targets, but Spring allocation bursts and cold-start behavior still need profiling.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Use them when SLOs justify CPU and memory headroom. Do canary rollouts because collector support varies by JDK version, base image, and observability tooling.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architect Perspective

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Choose ZGC for modern low-latency support on mainstream JDKs, Shenandoah when your distribution supports it well, and G1 when operational simplicity is more valuable.

Part 17

Decision Matrix

Situation Prefer Avoid Rationale
Default Spring Boot service G1GC, bounded pools, GC logs, JFR readiness Large unbounded heap Balanced operations and predictable defaults
Strict tail latency ZGC/Shenandoah evaluation Throughput-only tuning Concurrent collectors reduce long pauses
Memory-dense container MaxRAMPercentage, direct-memory cap, thread control -Xmx equal to limit Prevents RSS OOMKill
Unknown incident jcmd, JFR, dumps, GC logs Blind restart Preserves root-cause evidence
Part 18

Comparison Tables

Area Strength Tradeoff Best Use
G1GC Balanced default, compaction, pause target More metadata and tuning nuance General server services
ZGC/Shenandoah Very low pauses More CPU/headroom and version sensitivity Large heaps and strict p99/p999
Parallel GC High throughput Longer pauses Batch and offline jobs
JFR/async-profiler Production insight Needs process and storage controls Incident and optimization work
Part 19

Common Mistakes

  • Tuning flags without GC logs, JFR, or load-test evidence.
  • Ignoring non-heap memory in Kubernetes.
  • Treating average latency as success while p99 violates the SLO.
  • Taking heap dumps on overloaded nodes without planning disk and pause impact.
  • Changing multiple JVM variables at once and losing causality.

  5. How would you prove that a JVM tuning change improved p99 latency without increasing risk?

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

JVM tuning is the evidence-driven adjustment of memory, GC, JIT, threads, containers, and diagnostics to meet a workload-specific SLO.

Production JVM Feedback Loop
Metrics -> Logs -> JFR/Profile -> Hypothesis -> One Change -> Load Test -> Rollout/Runbook
Part 2

History

Tuning moved from hand-sizing generations and PermGen to collector selection, container ergonomics, observability defaults, and workload replay.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Random flag cargo-culting creates fragile services. Symptoms include pod OOMKills, long GC pauses, slow warmup, code cache saturation, direct-memory leaks, and thread exhaustion.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java exposes tuning controls because one runtime must support batch jobs, low-latency APIs, memory-constrained pods, huge heaps, and startup-sensitive serverless workloads.

Part 5

Internal Working

Tuning changes thresholds, reserved/committed memory, GC trigger points, compiler behavior, stack sizes, direct memory caps, and logging surfaces.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

Modern HotSpot ergonomics are good starting points. The architect job is to set constraints, capture evidence, and override defaults only where the workload proves it needs it.

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 7

Memory Layout

Budget heap, metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct memory, native allocations, GC overhead, and OS page cache against container limits.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Define SLO -> capture baseline -> identify dominant resource -> change one variable -> run representative load -> compare p95/p99, CPU, RSS, GC, allocation, errors -> document.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For jvm tuning, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

Part 12

Code Examples

java -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=65 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 \
  -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar

Diagnostic example:

java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar app.jar
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Baseline flags: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65, -XX:+UseG1GC, -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log, -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=/tmp/app.jfr,settings=profile.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Spring Boot tuning often starts with startup/warmup, connection pools, executor pools, cache sizes, JSON allocation, and actuator/JFR observability.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

In Kubernetes, align JVM flags with requests/limits. CPU throttling can look like GC or JIT failure, so inspect cgroup metrics alongside JVM metrics.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architect Perspective

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Tune for the constraint that matters: memory density, throughput, p99 latency, startup, or operational simplicity. Do not optimize all simultaneously.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why Java Provides This5Internal Working6JVM Implementation7Memory Layout8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Time Complexity11Space Complexity12Code Examples13Real Production Examples14Spring Boot Usage15Microservice Usage16Architect Perspective17Decision Matrix18Comparison Tables19Common Mistakes20Interview Questions21Revision Sheet22Summary Table
Part 1

Concept

Profiling measures where the JVM spends CPU, allocates memory, blocks threads, triggers GC, and waits on I/O so optimization starts from evidence.

Production JVM Feedback Loop
Metrics -> Logs -> JFR/Profile -> Hypothesis -> One Change -> Load Test -> Rollout/Runbook
Part 2

History

Java profiling evolved from intrusive agents and thread dumps to async-profiler, Java Flight Recorder, JDK Mission Control, continuous profilers, and production-safe sampling.

Part 3

Problem Statement

Without profiling, teams optimize guesses. Common misses include allocation hot spots, lock contention, logging overhead, regex backtracking, serialization costs, and native CPU outside Java frames.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides profiling hooks, JFR events, MXBeans, and diagnostic commands so production systems can be understood without always reproducing failures locally.

Part 5

Internal Working

Sampling profilers interrupt or observe threads periodically; allocation profilers record allocation sites; JFR emits structured low-overhead runtime events; async-profiler uses perf/async stack walking where available.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot exposes JFR, jcmd, safepoint stats, compiler data, heap histograms, thread dumps, and native memory tracking. Each has overhead and permission implications.

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=incident settings=profile duration=120s filename=/tmp/incident.jfr
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
jmap -histo:live <pid>
Part 7

Memory Layout

Profiling data itself consumes buffers and files. Allocation profiling can increase overhead; JFR ring buffers and disk rotation should be sized deliberately.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Define question -> select profiler -> capture during representative window -> inspect flame graph/JFR -> form hypothesis -> change code or config -> validate with same workload.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For profiling, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Part 10

Time Complexity

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space Complexity

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

Part 12

Code Examples

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=incident settings=profile delay=0s duration=120s filename=/tmp/incident.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.check

Diagnostic example:

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=incident settings=profile duration=120s filename=/tmp/incident.jfr
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
jmap -histo:live <pid>
Part 13

Real Production Examples

Commands: jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=profile settings=profile filename=/tmp/app.jfr, jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l, async-profiler -e cpu -d 60 -f cpu.html <pid>.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Part 14

Spring Boot Usage

Profile controllers, filters, serialization, database calls, cache serialization, and security chains. Spring abstractions are useful but can hide expensive reflection or proxy paths.

  • Prefer executable-jar testing for classpath and startup behavior.
  • Export Micrometer JVM metrics: heap, non-heap, GC pauses, threads, classes, and buffer pools.
  • Keep actuator diagnostic endpoints protected and disabled from public networks.
Part 15

Microservice Usage

Continuous profiling is valuable in microservices because hot paths shift with traffic mix, feature flags, and downstream behavior.

  • Align resources.requests and resources.limits with JVM memory flags.
  • Track pod OOMKill separately from Java OutOfMemoryError.
  • Warm up critical services before sending full traffic when JIT, caches, or connection pools matter.
Part 16

Architect Perspective

Architectural decisions should tie JVM behavior to SLOs, deployment topology, team maturity, and observability. A flag set copied from another service is not architecture; a measured policy with rollback and runbook support is.

Use JFR for broad JVM events, async-profiler for CPU/allocation flame graphs, heap dumps for retained memory, and thread dumps for blocking/deadlock.

Part 1

Concept

JVM troubleshooting is the disciplined incident process for turning symptoms like OOM, deadlock, high CPU, latency, crashes, or GC storms into evidence and fixes.

Production JVM Feedback Loop
Metrics -> Logs -> JFR/Profile -> Hypothesis -> One Change -> Load Test -> Rollout/Runbook
Part 2

History

Java operations matured from reading logs and heap dumps manually to JFR, unified logging, container metrics, continuous profiling, automated dump capture, and SRE runbooks.

Part 3

Problem Statement

During incidents, teams lose time by restarting before collecting evidence, confusing container OOMKill with Java OOME, or chasing application logs while JVM signals identify the issue.

Part 4

Why Java Provides This

Java provides diagnostic commands, structured runtime events, dumps, and flags because managed runtimes can expose rich state safely when production is degraded.

Part 5

Internal Working

Troubleshooting maps symptom to subsystem: CPU to threads/JIT/native, memory to heap/metaspace/direct/native, latency to GC/locks/I/O, crash to hs_err and native frames.

Part 6

JVM Implementation

HotSpot writes hs_err_pid*.log on fatal errors, supports jcmd, heap dumps on OOME, JFR, NMT, unified GC logs, and attach-based diagnostics if enabled.

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=incident settings=profile duration=120s filename=/tmp/incident.jfr
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
jmap -histo:live <pid>
Part 7

Memory Layout

Always separate heap committed, heap used, RSS, metaspace, direct buffers, native memory, and container limits. The failing layer determines the fix.

  • Container note: reserve memory for heap plus non-heap areas; never set -Xmx equal to the pod memory limit unless native headroom is intentionally handled.
Part 8

Execution Flow

Stabilize -> capture evidence -> classify failure -> reduce blast radius -> fix immediate trigger -> identify root cause -> add guardrails and alerts.

Part 9

Performance Analysis

For jvm troubleshooting, measure the symptom before choosing a flag. Useful signals include p95/p99 latency, allocation rate, GC pause distribution, safepoint time, CPU throttling, RSS, and warmup behavior.

Production baseline:
- Enable GC logs with rotation.
- Keep JFR available for short incident captures.
- Compare results under representative concurrency and payload sizes.

Most JVM mechanisms are not expressed as application Big-O, but the runtime cost scales with events: number of loaded classes, bytecodes executed, live objects scanned, stack frames walked, threads sampled, or regions collected. Architecturally, reduce the scaling dimension rather than memorizing a single formula.

Part 11

Space grows with live objects, class metadata, compiled methods, thread count, direct buffers, and diagnostic buffers. In containers, treat RSS as the budget and explicitly account for heap and non-heap memory.

java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps \
  -XX:ErrorFile=/dumps/hs_err_pid%p.log \
  -XX:StartFlightRecording=dumponexit=true,filename=/dumps/app.jfr,settings=profile \
  -jar app.jar

Diagnostic example:

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=incident settings=profile duration=120s filename=/tmp/incident.jfr
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
jmap -histo:live <pid>

Commands: jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l, jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, jstack <pid>, jmap -histo:live <pid>.

A realistic incident pattern is: a new release changes allocation, classpath, or traffic shape; the service passes functional tests; under production concurrency the JVM signal reveals the true bottleneck. Capture evidence before restarting whenever possible.

Spring Boot Actuator, Micrometer, heap dump endpoints, JFR integration, and structured logs speed diagnosis, but sensitive endpoints must be secured.

Automate evidence capture for OOME and crashes, keep GC/JFR on by default at acceptable overhead, and define restart policies that preserve diagnostic files.
